synthesis_description: All three agents converged on a third path beyond the binary: John should use a taxonomy of discomfort types (epistemic friction, social exposure, identity-based distress) to empirically assess Alice's situation, engage her privately, and refine his pedagogical delivery without abandoning intellectual challenge—recognising that Alice's full participation benefits the entire classroom community.
points_of_disagreement: Whether John's 'paternalism' framing is a genuine analytical concern or a sophisticated rationalisation for dismissing Alice's report without real investigation.
Whether there is a ceiling to Action C—i.e., whether some versions of Alice's distress may ultimately be irreconcilable with the course's pedagogical mission.
The degree to which institutional structures (HR, ombudsperson, formal complaints) should be proactively invoked versus treated as a last resort.
summary: All three agents independently rejected the original binary (continue unchanged vs. fully capitulate) and converged on a novel 'reflective adaptive refinement' path. The central analytical tool driving this consensus was a three-category taxonomy of student discomfort—epistemic friction, social exposure, and identity-based distress—which all parties recognised as the empirical hinge on which any sound recommendation must turn. John acknowledged his 'paternalism' framing could become a blind spot; Marcus contributed the insight that Alice's disengagement imposes a cost on the whole classroom, not just herself; and the external advisor added a structured sequence of professional obligations. Minor disagreements remained around whether a ceiling exists beyond which adjustment cannot resolve the conflict, and how aggressively to involve institutional mechanisms, but these did not undermine the core convergence.
